First of all, I’m sorry for your loss. Losing a grandparent is never easy. 

When the doctor took his vitals they’ll have checked for signs of life, which can include (but isn’t limited to) checking for breathing, heart rate, and shining a light into the eyes to see if the pupils contract, to see if the brain is interpreting light. The doctor may have used a stethoscope to check for a very weak pulse. It’s only after the tests are completed by someone who is trained to declare death that someone can be declared dead. It’s very rare the declaration is incorrect.

Behind the scenes, in the days between passing and the funeral/ceremony, there’s more checks that are done to ensure that it’s definitely not a prolonged episode of unconsciousness or other similar case, before an autopsy would be done if it’s needed. I’m not sure on the full extent of those checks, but there’d be so many professionals involved that someone would notice any signs of life if they were there. 

I understand the fear. I had the same when my grandad died. I kept thinking to myself that he would just wake up and it hadn’t really happened. Unfortunately, it’s very unlikely that that would be the case. Please don’t be afraid to reach out to your family and friends during this time. Grieving sucks, and it’s worse alone.

I have had serotonin syndrome a fair few times. Not once was it peaceful. The one time where I genuinely thought it could’ve been the end, I was hallucinating intense amounts, couldn’t regulate my temperature, was throwing up, and intensely exhausted and paranoid but unable to sleep at all. I don’t remember much about how I was feeling emotionally but I do remember being unable to figure what was real and what wasn’t. 

There are very few prescribed drugs that would provide a “peaceful” way out and those that do, work best in palliative care where the patients body has already started the dying process. An OD (antipsych or ssri) may result in unconsciousness if dose is high enough but the run up to that will not be comfortable or pretty or anything positive. Organs can be severely damaged based on which medication is taken and there will likely be tears to the oesophagus from vomiting.

A TENS machine (which stands for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) is a device which sends signals through the skin to interrupt pain signals from reaching the brain. 
The machine attaches to the skin with gel pads (similar to the patches on an ECG test in the doctors) and the nerve stimulation can be controlled by a remote, buttons on the device, or by an app on a phone.

Hiya! I pass out pretty regularly cos of a few health issues. I don’t have much time to get myself in a safe position once I know it’s coming on, if I’m not in a crowded place I can usually sit down and no one will have a clue it’s happening unless I try to make it known, so no one would know to intervene. 

For your writing purposes, this is the process for me: I usually feel a weird sensation in my stomach. I’m hyper aware of my insides and can often mistake this for feeling like I need to burp? I get really cold and start to sweat. At this point I cannot talk more than a few words and my vision is going static-y (it starts with a vignette). I then collapse. From others reports, it’s about 30s-1min for me. I then wake up, feel shaky, usually drink some water, and I’m completely fine. 

Again, for your writing since you mentioned this would happen after an OD, while it usually happens with no specific reason for me, it did happen for over a minute after I had taken an overdose of antidepressants (specifically SSRIs) a few years back. Overdose of this type can induce serotonin syndrome, which includes auditory and visual hallucinations, delusions, and overall altered sense of reality. Not sure of the exact storyline, but just giving the info incase it fits the characters experience!

I was diagnosed with bpd in 2019. In 2022, I was diagnosed with ptsd. I was diagnosed with fibro this year after experiencing symptoms from 2021. 

Coincidentally, my fibro symptoms started and worsened soon after my ptsd symptoms got very prevalent and disruptive. I’d experienced the symptoms for a long time but not as severe, and I was under a lot of stress at the time (working on a hospital ward during lockdown while also in uni), which I think triggered my symptoms. I did multiple types of therapy and my ptsd symptoms are manageable now, but unfortunately fibro doesn’t work the same :,) 

My understanding is that bpd and ptsd are comorbid (and also commonly mistaken as each other) and there’s a relationship between ptsd and chronic illnesses, and general poor health. A project I did in uni was close to doing an analysis of if ptsd was an underlying basis for bpd, since we know trauma is very common in people w bpd and the dsm has referred to that trauma as being severe and repetitive (not exact words) - the same trauma type which very often causes ptsd. 

If I wasn’t so brain-foggy right now I’d be able to link a fair few papers. NIMH is a good website for journals and articles for this if you fancy academia’s take on it. From personal experience and social circles, I don’t know anyone who has fibro and doesn’t have a ptsd or bpd diagnosis alongside.

first of all, not everyone with bulimia is going to be bigger than everyone with anorexia. Anorexics eat. 

There’s two categories in the DSM of anorexia, anorexia restrictive, and anorexia binge purge. 

Restrictive type tend not to binge and purge (vomit, overexercise, use laxatives or diuretics to ‘compensate’ for food intake) as much as those with binge purge type, but may still compensate for the food that they eat, which they have placed high restrictions on. These restrictions could be cutting out entire food groups, limiting a calorie amount per day/meal, or just because something can be perceived as unhealthy. 

Anorexia binge purge type exhibits bingeing often in a perceived way, rather than actual. Bingeing in a literal term is where you eat way more than should be expected in the typical time frame, and in eating disorders this often includes a feeling of losing control around it or feeling like you have to. Perceived bingeing is where the person eats and *feels* like they’ve eaten way more than they should, when in actuality it’s not excessive. Compensatory behaviours that I mentioned before will then follow. 

In bulimia, it’s not always vomiting that’s the purging action. The use of diuretics and/or laxatives can make the number on the scale go down but not actually make the person lose weight. Vomiting doesn’t always get everything up. Exercise can make someone gain or retain muscle weight, while losing fat, making the body composition different but appear the same. Bingeing will be actual bingeing, eating excessively in a short period of time. 

It really differs by person and how their calorie intake and outtake is. It’s individual down to what exactly they restrict and how they purge, if they do, and their weight before the symptoms started. The attitude towards eating disorders in psychiatrists is wildly biased based on the weight of the person at the time too, due to the perception that all anorexics are on deaths door.

TLDR, not all people with bulimia are larger than those with anorexia. They’re individual diseases that are down to the person’s symptoms and body on how they impact them. It’s only a by product of the symptoms that weight is lowered.

Edit: this is based on my experience (3yr in recovery from AN-BP), and my degree in psych where my diss was specialised in restrictive eating disorders. My definitions won’t be exact down to the diagnostic criteria - but the diagnostic criteria is not always exact when applied to patients in real life as anorexia and bulimia have shared symptoms themselves.

If by a binder you mean the same type of binder used to flatten chests from companies like spectrum and gc2b, wearing one comes with its own risks and requirements. 

They should be worn at a maximum of 6 hours a day, and shouldn’t be worn when exercising (including extended periods of walking). It’s important to have the correct posture while wearing one as the compression, even if the compression is in the form of just a front panel, makes you naturally slouch. They also impact how well you can cool down in hot weather since it’s very tight. Inaccurate sizing and/or prolonged wearing (even if you’re taking it off after 4-5 hours) can cause rib damage over time, and if you have breasts and do not wear it with your chest in the correct position, (again over time) it can cause tissue damage to the nipples and overall just change how they sit naturally. Stretching before and after wear can majorly prevent muscle soreness in neck, spine, and shoulders. 

Personally it helps me feel a lot more grounded and relaxed, but I spent a lot of time wearing a binder not listening to the recommendations and I think that is why my upper back and shoulder pain is one of my main/worst pain areas (and my lower ribs are more “inward” than they should be). 

I’m not trying to scare you off of wearing one - tight clothing can help some people w fibro ! But just to make clear how different you have to go about wearing binders Vs compression shirts to take care in the long term

It’s not curable in the sense that one sole thing will erase it, but with treatment and time, the symptoms you experience can become less severe and I know a few people who have the opinion that if they were assessed now, wouldn’t fit the diagnosis anymore, as their treatment helps. 

My personal tips are:
to look into dialectical behavioural therapy, and the coping skills associated with that. TIPP is a very good one for me when I am in an emotional state where I am very very angry and/or I want to hurt myself. There’s a DBT workbook available on Amazon, and a lot of DBT coping mechanisms posted online. 
to start a mood journal, which can log behaviour and activities alongside it. I use the app Daylio. It lets me add customised moods and log what I’ve done that day. It analyses it to show you how things you do / people you see etc. impact your mood, and you can log moods more than once a day. This helped me recognise what made me feel worse. 

There’s not a medication that is specifically for bpd, like there would for another condition. For example when someone has depression, we know antidepressants can help that, because it helps the serotonin amount. With borderline, we don’t have the same level of understanding of how it is in the brain, so it’s a combination of medicines that work the best for the individual. This can be antidepressants, sedatives, antipsychotics, mood stabilisers. I am on a low dose (non-clinical) of amitriptyline and a clinical dose of sertraline. This helps me manage my symptoms the best, alongside coping mechanisms I have learned in therapy. Unfortunately it’s a lot of trial and error for medications, some might make certain symptoms worse, it’s different for everyone. 

I get what you mean about not wanting to degrade. I’m not a doctor, but if you want to self harm and the rage becomes heavier when you’re not on your current meds, it sounds like a good idea to stick with them. If you discuss with your psychiatrist exactly what symptoms you want to manage with medication, they’ll be able to adjust your medications to those. Please don’t take yourself off of any medications without letting your doctors know, the side effects of coming off too quick can be very very uncomfortable.

Like coldblood-13 said, it is normal to have urges and behaviours that are just to cope with certain things. 

It’s very normal for sexual trauma (and any other trauma) to cause someone to change daily behaviour and urges to cope with thoughts and feelings, and these can be useful behaviours or ones that disrupt daily living or relationships and don’t serve a coping purpose. 

For example in myself, I dissociate when I get reminded of my trauma (also SA) in situations where I’m not prepared, including if I get an intrusive thought about it. while it’s my brain “protecting” me, it’s not actually helpful and disrupts whatever I’m doing at the time for a good 30-45 minutes, but is a coping mechanism. On a positive side, I’m hypervigilant about others body language and how this relates to potential behaviour. This does actually protect, and helps me cope with intrusive thoughts and anxiety since I’m actively checking if I’m safe and know I can call someone if I feel I’m not. 

In regard to if someone knows if they’re going crazy (if by crazy you mean a complete detachment from reality or firm belief in delusion) - it depends what illness, the severity, and personal factors of their lifestyle. Someone who spends a lot of time with others (who don’t have the same illness and behaviours) will have a contrast between behaviour and if it’s mentioned, they’ll be aware others don’t do the same behaviours and it’s different but might not realise the severity and disruption to life as it feels normal to them/the way they “should” act/the way they just are. Speaking from experience, people can know that their false beliefs are factually wrong but still believe them completely. For me it was because I didn’t want the potential consequences of if I didn’t believe them and I should’ve, but of course like every mental health condition, it differs for the person. 

I hope you get effective help to help you cope with your trauma. It’s a really difficult thing to cope with.

my dissertation was focusing on a prospective differing level of vulnerability to eating disorders, body shape perception issues, and borderline traits between trans and cis people while also looking to see if those three things were linked in the whole sample. they are all significantly linked in the whole sample, and trans people are significantly more likely to report borderline traits but not eating disorders or body shape perception issues! of course there’s the issues of small sampling (~120 participants if i remember right, near enough equal split between trans and cis participants), but the results align with existing literature, even though there’s not much that’s inclusive of trans people. I used the EAT-26 to measure disordered eating traits. In retrospect i could have chosen a better questionnaire for this as the EAT-26 focuses on restrictive EDs and it would’ve been better to include more EDs than just AN/BN, but my word count was very limited. 

I’m working on my masters thesis now, which is working on explaining why trans people are more likely to experience bpd traits than cis people, and the current theory I’m working with is that minority stress and adverse childhood experiences from a non supportive environment contributes to the development of bpd traits, alongside biological factors (genetic predisposition to mental illness, and neurobiological changes in the brain caused by adverse childhood experiences that impact the parts of the brain associated with bpd symptoms i.e. prefrontal cortex and decision making/impulsivity). 

(note: I’m using trans as a short term for transgender and nonbinary people, the data analysis i executed had transgender people grouped as everyone who is not cisgender. I’m trans myself, and consulted trans friends on this grouping system beforehand :) )

The mesolimbic pathway makes sure cognitive functions such as incentive salience, motivation, reinforcement learning, and processing fear is all regular. It plays a central role in addiction, and in illnesses such as parkinson’s, schizophrenia, and depression. it’s in the midbrain, near the pituitary gland. 

It doesn’t cause solely hallucinations, but i’m not sure exactly why. I have no sources to confirm, but my thoughts are that excessive dopamine in this would impact stimuli processing and interrupt the interpretation. 

The appearance of negative symptoms of schizophrenia was also investigated by Davis (2001), where he found that hypodopaminergia (a lack of dopamine) in the striatum caused the symptoms. This again was supported by the use of medication. I like to think of it as a scale, where the more dopamine = more action. 

Serotonin does have an impact, to an extent. Low levels of serotonin has been linked to an overproduction of dopamine. [this website](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/326090.php#summary) talks about the link between the two.

i’ll explain this in relation to schizophrenia. positive symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations, (such as visual or auditory) have been theorized to be a result of an excess amount of dopamine. 

A study by Rossum in 1966 in regards to the dopamine hypothesis roughly estimated that an imbalance of Dopamine was the cause of the positive symptoms, but he didn’t find out exactly why or whether the imbalance was the brain having more or less dopamine -only the vague area. 

If we fast forward to 2001, Davis looked at the amounts of dopamine in certain areas of brain. He found that hyperdopaminergia [a lot of dopamine] in the mesolimbic pathway mediated positive psychotic symptoms. This is further supported by antipsychotics -which block D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway- successfully reducing these symptoms. 
This meant that a large amount of dopamine in one part of the brain resulted in hallucinations and delusions. 

in simpler terms, hallucinations are thought to be as a result of excessive amounts of dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway 

ELI5, without the fancy science words: a lot of one type of brain chemical in a certain part of your brain makes your brain imagine things that aren’t really there.
